messages.text: What are the main findings of this paper?

messages.short_answer: The paper reports that 10 non-expert participants explored prompts opportunistically rather than systematically, and struggled in ways that echo end-user programming and interactive machine learning studies. Human-to-human instruction expectations and a tendency to overgeneralize from few observations were key barriers.

sections.title: Core findings from the abstract and introduction
sections.text: The authors report that participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and that barriers included expectations from human-to-human instruction and a tendency to overgeneralize. The introduction states that participants struggled to make robust, systematic progress, and that the paper makes three contributions: the tool, a rich description of non-expert struggles, and opportunities for tool design and education.

sections.title: Specific behavioural findings from the user study
sections.text: According to the overview of the study pages, most participants declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing, with none using the systematic prompt testing interface. Participants also favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing and struggled more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts.

sections.title: Why this matters for your user study
sections.text: Your planned study of how non-experts write prompts overlaps with the paper's think-aloud, 10-participant design probe. You could consider whether your measures capture the behaviours reported here, such as premature success declaration, over-generalization, and role confusion, and how your sample differs from the paper's STEM-skewed, academic early-adopter pool.

sources.text: These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. The pages also cover participants struggling to explain why prompts worked or failed across contexts, and a finding that participants favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing, with the authors linking this to early childhood education literature.

These pages describe the participant table and the interview protocol for a study where participants used the BotDesigner tool to improve a baseline chatbot so it could mimic a conversational style seen in a cooking video. Participants (ten people with varied professions and LLM knowledge) were shown an episode of Back to Back Chef and a transcript with color-coded highlights of humor, analogies, concept simplification, and step confirmation. They had up to one hour to prompt the bot toward these behaviors, with the researchers observing approach rather than final quality, and offering prompt suggestions only after participants got stuck for several minutes. Researchers also reminded participants of labeling, systematic error testing, and edit/replay functions when relevant. Figure 3 shows the opening turns of the expert-amateur cooking transcript used as the target.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

sections.title: Study setup and participants
sections.text: The authors used BotDesigner as a design probe and observed 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience doing a chatbot design task. Participants had varying programming and chatbot design experience, and the authors state their pool was skewed toward STEM professionals and graduate students.

sections.title: Procedure and analysis as described
sections.text: Participants were asked to think aloud, and the authors then ran exploratory data analysis on transcribed videos. They coded which prompt design approaches were attempted, when participants seemed to struggle, and where interviewers intervened. During the study, interviewers offered prompt suggestions based on prompt design research after an initial phase, and not all participants received the same advice.

sources.text: This excitement around LLMs and prompting is propelling a rapidly growing set of LLM-powered applications [23] and prompt design tools [3, 20, 32]. Yet despite widespread excitement, surprisingly little is known about how non-experts intuitively approach designing prompts with LLM-and-prompt-based tools, and how efective they are in doing so. While prompting LLMs can appear efortless, designing efective prompting strategies requires identifying the contexts in which these LLMs’ errors arise, devising prompting strategies to overcome them, and systematically assessing those strategies’ efectiveness. These tasks fall on so-called “prompt engineers”— the designers, domain experts, and any other end-user or professional attempting to improve an LLM’s output—and are challenging tasks even for LLM experts, as well as topics of ongoing research in Natural Language Processing (NLP) [7, 30, 42]. Prompt design tools to date have focused on supporting professional programmers [45] and NLP practitioners [42], rather than non-AI experts, non-programmers, and other potential end-users of these systems.

sources.text: These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. The pages also cover participants struggling to explain why prompts worked or failed across contexts, and a finding that participants favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing, with the authors linking this to early childhood education literature.

These pages describe the participant table and the interview protocol for a study where participants used the BotDesigner tool to improve a baseline chatbot so it could mimic a conversational style seen in a cooking video. Participants (ten people with varied professions and LLM knowledge) were shown an episode of Back to Back Chef and a transcript with color-coded highlights of humor, analogies, concept simplification, and step confirmation. They had up to one hour to prompt the bot toward these behaviors, with the researchers observing approach rather than final quality, and offering prompt suggestions only after participants got stuck for several minutes. Researchers also reminded participants of labeling, systematic error testing, and edit/replay functions when relevant. Figure 3 shows the opening turns of the expert-amateur cooking transcript used as the target.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

It is worth noting that although BotDesigner enables this full workfow, we do not necessarily expect all end-users to engage in all its steps. However, we did validate BotDesigner’s functionality and usability throughout this workfow via a set of pilot user studies (see Appendix A.3 for details) to ensure that these pieces are available should users choose to systematically assess their prompt designs. 3.3 User Study Design To understand how end users intuitively approach prompt design, we invited 10 non-expert prompt designers to use BotDesigner and think-aloud. We invited the participants to improve upon a baseline chatbot template towards given goals (see Tasks below), while we observed and took note of the various prompt design approaches and testing strategies they engaged in. We chose the task of improving a chatbot, instead of creating it from scratch, in order to avoid the Blank Page Syndrome, the efect where users staring at a blank page do not know where to begin. We chose to create a design probe because the robustness of prompt strategies is highly dependent on specifc conversational contexts, as is users’ ability to create prompts and debug. Enabling people to engage in designing LLM-and-prompt-based chatbots hands-on offers deeper insights than conducting interviews about hypothetical scenarios alone. We chose to purpose-build a prompt design tool because existing tools focus on enabling non-experts to experiment with various prompting strategies rather than crafting robust and generalizable prompts. 3.1 Designing a No-Code Prompt Design Tool as Probe Design Goals. We have two goals in designing BotDesigner: First, to enable end-users, without any prompt design experience or even programming or ML experience, to (i) create a chatbot using prompts, without code, and (ii) systematically evaluate their prompts. Second, to allow end-users to engage in this process in a fexible, open-ended way, allowing us to observe their intuitive behaviors and thought processes.

3 METHOD: DESIGN PROBE In this work, we aim to understand how non-experts intuitively approach designing robust prompts, and whether and how they struggle in doing so. We want to dive deep into what those struggles reveal about people’s assumptions and understanding of promptbased systems in order to inform how end-user-facing prompt design tools might best support their users. We chose to investigate these questions in the context of designing instructional chatbots—chatbots that walk users through an activity (e.g., cooking a recipe, fxing a wif connection) while answering user questions and engaging in social conversation as needed. Chatbot tasks are sufciently open-ended that they open the door to a wide variety of types of problems and prompt-based solution approaches. Instructional chatbots represent a common chatbot use case (e.g., customer service bots), and their constituent tasks are some of the tasks that GPT-3 peforms more efectively out-of-the-box.

Two of the authors then compared these approaches across participants and categorized their struggles using afnity diagrams [34] and by creating a service blueprint [5] that documents the specifc approaches individual participants attempt.
